questions.question: In networking, 1U and 2U primarily describe:
options: Rack height of a fixed switch (1 or 2 rack units)—affecting port density, power, and cooling in a rack
questions.explanation: Pizza-box leaves are commonly 1U; denser systems may be 2U.

questions.question: High port density in a 1U pizza-box matters at scale because:
options: More servers per rack switch reduces tiers/cost—but raises power, thermals, and blast radius of one box
Density replaces the need for redundancy
questions.explanation: Design tradeoff: density vs failure domain and power.

questions.question: Redundant power supplies / hot-swap FRUs improve platform reliability by:
options: Surviving PSU failure and enabling field replacement without full chassis loss—when designed and monitored correctly
Removing the need for dual uplinks

questions.question: Front-to-back airflow and rack orientation matter because:
options: Mismatched airflow causes thermal throttling/failures that look like 'random' packet loss or reloads
questions.explanation: Physical ops is part of platform sustainability.

questions.question: In a modular chassis, the supervisor engine typically owns:
options: Control-plane functions (routing protocols, management) while line cards forward most data-plane traffic in hardware
All packet forwarding exclusively in software forever
questions.explanation: Supervisor = control; line cards + fabric = forwarding path.

questions.question: Line cards in a chassis primarily provide:
options: Port interfaces and local packet processing/lookup toward the fabric—scaling port count modularly
questions.explanation: Modular architecture = insert line cards for density.

questions.question: Chassis fabric modules / backplane exist to:
options: Switch cells/packets between line cards at high bandwidth with scheduling to avoid internal congestion
questions.explanation: Internal fabric is the chassis datapath.

questions.question: A fixed-configuration pizza-box differs from a modular chassis mainly by:
options: Non-expandable integrated ports/ASICs in one box vs slot-based supervisors/line cards/fabric

questions.question: Dual supervisors with failover aim to:
options: Keep control plane available through supervisor failure—ideally with minimal forwarding disruption if NSF/NSR/ISSU capabilities exist
questions.explanation: Control-plane HA; forwarding continuity depends on platform features.

questions.question: Best distinction among planes:
options: Control plane computes reachability (RIB); forwarding/data plane uses hardware tables (FIB/adjacency) to move packets
They are three names for SNMP only
Forwarding plane only runs OSPF hellos
questions.explanation: Interview staple: control vs forwarding/data plane.

questions.question: RIB vs FIB (forwarding table):
options: RIB holds routing-protocol knowledge; FIB/hardware forwarding table is what the ASIC uses for lookups
They are always byte-identical with no install filters
RIB is only on the optics
questions.explanation: Policy/NH issues can leave RIB≠FIB behavior.

questions.question: A switch ASIC’s job in the forwarding plane is to:
options: Perform high-speed parse, lookup, buffer/schedule, and rewrite in hardware so most packets never hit the CPU
questions.explanation: ASICs = merchant or custom silicon pipelines.

questions.question: Merchant silicon + whitebox/SONiC-style platforms emphasize:
options: Standard ASICs with open/disaggregated NOS options—ops must own integration, imaging, and support models

questions.question: CAM/TCAM matter in platforms because:
options: They enable fast exact/ternary lookups (MAC, routes, ACLs)—capacity limits become scale/feature constraints

questions.question: MAC learning/forwarding on a switch:
options: Maps source MACs to ports/tunnels and forwards/floods based on destination MAC—bridging domain design affects blast radius
MAC is only used by BGP
MAC tables are infinite and never age
Rewriting IP TTL updates the MAC table
questions.explanation: L2 fundamentals still appear in fabric edge/host attachment.

questions.question: ARP’s role in packet delivery on Ethernet/IP is:
options: Resolve next-hop IP to MAC so L2 can deliver the frame toward the next hop

questions.question: A typical L3 hop rewrite includes:
options: Decrement TTL (or hop limit), update L2 header to next-hop MAC, and transmit on the chosen egress—after FIB lookup
Strip IP and send raw TCP only
Change the source IP randomly each hop
questions.explanation: Lookup → rewrite → TTL is core packet-flow literacy.

questions.question: TTL/hop-limit exists primarily to:
options: Bound forwarding loops by expiring packets that circulate too long
questions.explanation: Loop safety in the data plane.

questions.question: Cut-through forwarding can start egress earlier than store-and-forward, but:
options: Speed mismatch, errors, or feature needs often force store-and-forward behavior—latency wins are situational

questions.question: Control-plane policing (CoPP) protects platforms by:
options: Rate-limiting/filtering traffic punted to the CPU so floods don’t melt routing/management
questions.explanation: Keep forwarding in ASIC; protect supervisors/CPU.

questions.question: In large-scale DC fabrics, BGP is often preferred as underlay because:
options: Policy control, horizontal scale, and ECMP friendliness (e.g., eBGP per leaf) versus IGP flooding limits
BGP only works on the public internet

questions.question: OSPF/IS-IS as IGPs are typically stronger when you need:
options: Fast interior topology awareness within an AS—with area/scaling design—versus policy-heavy interdomain BGP
WAN-only with no LAN use ever

questions.question: ECMP forwarding depends on:
options: Multiple equal-cost next hops installed in the FIB and a hash over flow keys to pick a member

questions.question: BFD aids routing reliability by:
options: Detecting path failure faster than protocol hellos alone—enabling quicker withdrawal/shift with false-positive tradeoffs

questions.question: Graceful restart / NSR features target:
options: Reducing forwarding disruption during control-plane restarts/failover when peers/helpers cooperate

questions.question: ISSU / hitless upgrade aspirations matter operationally because:
options: Software upgrades are a major planned risk; platforms that preserve forwarding during upgrade reduce impact

questions.question: Shallow buffers favor low latency and high radix, but under congestion they:
options: Overflow quickly → drop or assert backpressure—so topology and congestion control must share the load
Expand to seconds of buffering automatically

questions.question: Deep buffers absorb bursts better but risk:
options: Higher latency and bufferbloat if queues grow large—TCP may slow only after long standing queues
Eliminating PFC needs forever with no tradeoffs

questions.question: Bufferbloat refers to:
options: Excessively large standing queues that inflate latency/jitter even when 'no drops' look healthy
Having zero buffers on a switch
questions.explanation: Reliability of platforms includes latency under load.

questions.question: Packet loss from congestion on oversubscribed or shallow paths typically causes:
options: TCP retransmits/throughput collapse and app timeouts—platforms need detection and capacity/QoS responses

questions.question: TCP congestion control reacts to loss/ECN by:
options: Reducing sending rate—so fabric drops/marks directly shape application throughput and latency

questions.question: Priority Flow Control (PFC) tries to:
options: Pause traffic classes to avoid drops (lossless-ish)—but can cause HOL blocking/deadlock if misused at scale
Always improve WAN TCP without risk

questions.question: ECN / DCQCN-style congestion control helps shallow fabrics by:
options: Marking/reacting before queues fully overflow—keeping latency and drops lower when endpoints cooperate
Removing the need for any capacity

questions.question: Microbursts matter even when average utilization looks fine because:
options: Short peaks exceed shallow buffers and cause loss/ECN while averages stay green

questions.question: Tail-drop vs WRED/ECN marking strategies differ in that:
options: Tail-drop drops at full queue; WRED/ECN can signal earlier to smooth TCP and avoid synchronized collapses

questions.question: Shared vs dedicated buffer pools trade:
options: Efficiency under uneven load (shared) versus isolation guarantees (dedicated)—mis-sizing causes unfair drops

questions.question: An oversubscribed link/tier means:
options: Potential demand exceeds provisioned bandwidth—contention appears under correlated load or failure
questions.explanation: Design must state oversub ratios explicitly.

questions.question: A non-blocking Clos ideal means:
options: Any idle input can reach any idle output at line rate given enough fabric capacity—real designs approximate with oversub choices

questions.question: LACP/LAG is used to:
options: Bundle links for capacity and some redundancy with member hashing—still watch hash polarization and member failure

questions.question: MLAG / dual-homed ToR pairs aim to:
options: Let hosts dual-attach across two switches without a single ToR as hard SPOF—when peer-link and consistency are solid
Merge two AZs into one failure domain intentionally

questions.question: ToR vs EoR/MoR placement is a platform/ops choice about:
options: Cable length, failure domain size, port utilization, and how you roll upgrades—tradeoffs, not one true religion

questions.question: Breakout (e.g., 400G→4×100G) and SerDes lanes matter because:
options: They change effective port count, oversub, and failure granularity—mis-cabling breaks designs
Breakout removes the need for FIB

questions.question: FEC on high-speed links is used to:
options: Correct bit errors so higher lane rates stay reliable—adding a small latency cost

questions.question: Jumbo frames / MTU consistency matters because:
options: MTU mismatches cause black holes or fragmentation pain across the fabric and overlays

questions.question: Underlay vs overlay in cloud fabrics:
options: Underlay provides IP multipath among switches; overlays (e.g., VXLAN) carry tenant networks on top—faults can be either layer

questions.question: Elephant vs mice flows affect ECMP/hash designs because:
options: Few long-lived elephants can polarize and congest a member while mice suffer—hashing and spraying strategies matter
All flows are equal size always

questions.question: Many-to-one incast into a shallow-buffered egress is dangerous because:
options: Aggregate arrival rate exceeds drain + buffer → loss/PFC storms impacting innocent flows

questions.question: An engineering mechanism for consistent platforms at scale is:
options: Role-based golden configs/images and automated conformance—so pizza-box fleets stay identical and reviewable

questions.question: VOQ architectures reduce head-of-line blocking by:
options: Queuing per destination so a hot egress less often stalls unrelated traffic across a chassis fabric

questions.question: Selecting network platforms for large-scale environments should explicitly weigh:
options: Form factor (1U/2U/chassis), ASIC/buffer model, port density, HA features, and ops mechanisms—not datasheet peak Gbps alone
Only the number of RJ45 serial ports

questions.question: Life of a packet — host to ToR (first hop) typically includes:
options: Frame leaves NIC with dest MAC of gateway/peer; ToR parses, learns/forwards at L2 or routes at L3 toward the fabric
The packet skips the ToR and appears magically at the destination AZ
Only DNS is consulted; no MAC or FIB lookup occurs
TTL is increased at the NIC before send
questions.explanation: Start of path: host → leaf/ToR attachment.

questions.question: Life of a packet — across a Clos/spine-leaf fabric after the leaf routes it:
options: Leaf does FIB lookup, rewrites L2 toward a chosen ECMP uplink; spine switches toward the destination leaf; egress leaf delivers to the host subnet
Every hop decrements the MAC address instead of TTL
Spines always flood every packet to all leaves like a hub
The packet is stored on the supervisor disk then emailed
questions.explanation: Fabric hops: lookup → rewrite → ECMP → destination leaf.

questions.question: Life of a packet — at each L3 hop the platform must at least:
options: Lookup the next hop in the forwarding table, rewrite L2 headers, decrement TTL/hop limit, then transmit (buffering if congested)
Only update BGP and drop the packet
Strip IP and forward raw TCP on a random port
Increment TTL and clear the FCS always
questions.explanation: Canonical hop: lookup → rewrite → TTL → schedule/transmit.
